name: Slagside Ironhand Welding Gauntlet
description:
Heavy split-leather gauntlets reinforced with ceramic fiber panels across the knuckles and dorsal hand, stitched in double-pass aramid thread. The wrist cuffs are wide and buckled with reclaimed steel hardware, scorched amber-brown from repeated heat exposure. Most pairs show carbon streaks and flux spatter that no cleaning removes — worn like a badge.

Lining is a single layer of reflective fiberglass batting, functional but unrefined. The thumb and index finger are reinforced with additional ceramic tile insets for arc-strike resistance. Sold in pairs, often resold individually on Shelf markets.
functionality: Rated for arc welding and open-flame exposure up to 900°C brief contact. Wide cuff protects the forearm gap common in aug-compatible sleeves. No haptic or electronic components — fully passive thermal protection.
what_it_says: This person works with fire and doesn't complain about it.
story_hooks: A pair of these gloves is found at a crime scene — the wearer left behind no prints, but the ceramic dust matches a specific batch sold only to one Shelf fabricator.
A Tier 3 inspector arrives at a factory floor and notices a worker's Slagside gauntlets have been modified with a hidden wire channel — someone's routing signal through the cuff.
related_entities: Kessler Kinetics Vaultstreak R7 Runner Leg

physical_description.visual_profile: Heavy-duty welding gauntlets with a brutalist silhouette — wide wrist cuffs that extend 4-5 inches up the forearm, tapering to articulated hand coverage. The overall impression is industrial and purposeful, scarred by legitimate use rather than aesthetic design. Worn by trade workers, salvage crews, and Iowan Behemoth maintenance techs.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and generous through the palm and fingers, with deliberate bulk at the knuckles and hand dorsum. The wrist cuff fits snug over a shirt sleeve but not constrictive. Designed for dexterity within heavy labor, not fashion.
physical_description.primary_material: Split leather (likely reclaimed bovine hide) with ceramic fiber reinforcement panels and embedded ceramic tile inserts. Double-pass aramid thread throughout. Reflective fiberglass batting lining.
physical_description.texture: Rough and tactile — the leather is scarred and heat-distressed with visible burnishing. Ceramic panels are slightly raised and rigid. Wrist cuffs show deep scoring and pitting from metal tool contact. Lining is soft but industrial-grade, matte reflective.
physical_description.color_scheme: Base scorched amber-brown leather with charcoal-gray ceramic panels. Carbon streaks and flux spatter in black and burnt orange create permanent marbling across the dorsal surface. Reclaimed steel hardware reads as gunmetal-gray with copper oxidation at edges.
physical_description.closures: Wide wrist cuffs secured with reclaimed steel buckles (typically 2-3 per gauntlet) — industrial friction-lock or pin-and-loop style. No magnetic snaps or tech-driven fasteners.
distinctive_features: Double-reinforced ceramic tile inserts on thumb and index finger for arc-strike resistance
Permanent carbon streaks and flux spatter — wear marks that become identity markers
Reflective fiberglass batting lining visible at wrist opening
Often resold individually, creating asymmetrical pairs on secondary markets
Hand-stitched repair patches visible on most worn pairs
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 4-5. Functional street-origin manufacturing. Affordable and durable, signaling blue-collar or sub-grade labor rather than wealth. A pair costs roughly 85-120 Φ on the Shelf.
physical_description.cultural_context: Wearing these signals a trade worker, salvage technician, Behemoth maintenance crew, or someone who works with heat and metal in ungoverned or semi-regulated zones. They are anti-fashion — a status symbol only to those who understand their necessity.
physical_description.condition_typical: Always weathered. Carbon and flux are permanent features, not defects. Most pairs show visible repair stitching, small holes patched with mismatched leather, and deep creasing at the knuckle and finger joints. Pristine gauntlets are suspicious and rarely trusted.
